content:
Yesterday we saw how Israel treated Yahweh with contempt. They refused His promises, forgot His works, accused Him of evil intentions, longed for Egypt, and wanted to silence His faithful witnesses. Today this same passage turns and searches us, for the story of Israel was written not only as history, but as a warning for the New Creation. We may never openly say that we despise God, and yet our actions can sometimes treat Him with the very same contempt that Israel showed. Let us look honestly at our own hearts.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we believe our fears more than His promises. Israel saw the giants and concluded that God could not give them the victory. In the same way, when we look at the giants in our own lives and say, "This problem is too great for God," we are making our circumstances greater than our God. The giant may be a sickness, a debt, a broken relationship, or a fear that will not leave us. It is not wrong to feel the weight of these things.

But when we decide that our trouble is bigger than God's power, we have quietly insulted Him, just as Israel did at the border of Canaan.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we accuse Him of having evil intentions toward us. In seasons of suffering, the heart may begin to whisper, "God does not care about me," or, "He has brought me here only to destroy me." These thoughts question His goodness instead of trusting His loving purpose.
Israel looked at the hand that had fed them and called it a hand of destruction. We can do the same when we look at a hard season and decide that God has turned against us, when in truth He may be leading us through that very valley toward a greater blessing.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we forget His former faithfulness.
How easily we forget the many times God has carried us through trials, answered our prayers, protected us from dangers we never even saw, provided for our needs, and strengthened us in our weakness. Then a new difficulty appears, and we behave as though He has never helped us before. Each new trouble finds us fearful again, as if the God who saved us a hundred times cannot be trusted the hundred and first time. This forgetfulness dishonours the One who has never once let us fall.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we continually grumble against His leading. Israel complained against Moses and Aaron, but their complaints were really directed at God, who had appointed them. We too may question God's guidance simply because the path He has chosen is difficult. When the road is hard, we begin to murmur, and though our words may be aimed at people or at circumstances, underneath it we are often complaining against the God who is leading us. A grumbling heart is rarely only about the difficulty. It is often a quiet accusation against the wisdom of God's leading.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we reject His Word and trust human opinions instead. Israel believed the report of the ten spies more than the promise of Yahweh. Today, many believers know very well what the Scriptures say, yet they allow the opinions of people, the wisdom of the world, or their own feelings to become more authoritative than the Word of God. When the voice of a man, or the voice of our own emotions, carries more weight in our decisions than the clear Word of God, we have placed something above Him, and that is contempt.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we long to return to Egypt.
Egypt represents the old life from which Christ has delivered us.When obedience becomes costly, the heart may begin to long for the former ways, forgetting the bondage from which God rescued us. We remember the pleasures but forget the chains. We remember the taste of the old life but forget the tears. To desire the very slavery from which Christ set us free is to treat His great salvation as though it were a small thing. And closely joined to this, we treat Yahweh with contempt when we seek another leader in place of Christ. Israel said, "Let us choose another leader and return to Egypt." Whenever we reject the leadership of Christ and instead surrender ourselves to the flesh, to the world, or to the adversary and his agencies, we are choosing another master. Christ alone has the right to lead the New Creation, and to hand ourselves over to any other guide is to despise the Shepherd God has given us.

We treat Yahweh with contempt when we refuse correction. Joshua and Caleb faithfully declared God's Word, yet the people wanted to silence them. In the same way, whenever the Scriptures expose our unbelief, we may resist the correction rather than humbly receive it. It is a serious thing when the truth comes to help us and we push it away because it wounds our pride. And finally, we treat Yahweh with contempt when we presume upon His mercy.

Israel experienced God's patience, forgiveness, and provision again and again, yet they continued in rebellion. His mercy was never meant to encourage disobedience. It was meant to lead His people to repentance. When we take His kindness as permission to keep sinning, we turn His mercy into an occasion for contempt.

But here we must be very careful and very tender, for there is a great difference between contempt and a genuine struggle of faith. A true believer may pass through fear, weakness, confusion, and unanswered questions, and still sincerely seek God through it all. That is not contempt. A trembling heart that still turns to God is precious to Him. Contempt is something else. Contempt is a settled attitude that continually refuses His Word, questions His goodness, and persists in unbelief in spite of repeated proofs of His faithfulness. So if today your heart is fearful but still reaching for God, do not condemn yourself. God is gentle with the struggling. The warning is not against the weak who still cling to Him. It is against the hardened heart that has decided it will not trust Him no matter what He does.

Therefore, let us examine our own hearts honestly. Do we trust God only when the path is easy? Do we obey Him only when His will happens to agree with our own desires? Do we magnify our giants while making His power look small? Do we remember Egypt more fondly than the freedom Christ has given us? May we never treat God as though His promises are uncertain, His power is limited, or His love is doubtful. Instead, let us honour Him by believing His Word, by remembering His faithfulness, by receiving His correction, and by following Christ with steadfast confidence, even when the giants still stand before us. For contempt begins the moment we make God small in our thoughts and make our fears great. Faith does the very opposite. Faith remembers who God is, believes what He has spoken, and follows Him even while the giants remain in plain sight, because it knows that the God who has been faithful in all our yesterdays will be just as faithful in every tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,
Search us honestly, and show us any hidden contempt we have shown toward You.

Forgive us for believing our fears above Your promises and our feelings above Your Word.

Keep us from longing for the Egypt You brought us out of, and from following any leader but Christ.

Where we have merely struggled in weakness, hold us gently, for we are still reaching for You.

Make our faith the kind that keeps its eyes on Your greatness while the giants still stand.

"Examine me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. Lead me along the path of everlasting life." Psalm 139:23-24

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
